extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Renaissance art history; art historians and conservators
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria used in Vasari-style Lives for judging the technical quality, style, conservation, and reputation of Renaissance panel and fresco painting. Useful for evaluating workmanship, materials, composition, and historical influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifelike heads / portraits from life
rubrics_metrics.description: Pietro produced an 'infinite number of different heads, many of them portrayed from life,' and certain heads were judged by 'the most experienced craftsmen to be the best thing that Pietro ever made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges value naturalistic, individualized heads drawn from life; lifelike portraiture was considered a mark of excellence (example: frieze with life-size heads praised as his best work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape realism and 'true method' of landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'made therein a landscape that was then held most beautiful, because the true method of making them... had not yet been seen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A convincing, novel treatment of landscape (accurate receding space, believable terrain and atmosphere) was a distinct praise-worthy technical achievement in the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical painting practice: layer timing and cracking
rubrics_metrics.description: The panels 'have suffered considerably, and they are all cracked in the dark parts and where there are shadows; and this comes to pass when the first coat of colour... is worked on before it is thoroughly dry,' causing cracks as the layers dry through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper timing between layers (allowing ground/first coat to dry before subsequent coats) is a technical requirement to avoid later cracking; knowledge of medium-specific drying behaviour is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive naturalism (pose and emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Christ in the Garden Pietro 'showed how well sleep can prevail over pains and discomforts, having represented them asleep in attitudes of perfect ease.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalistic poses and emotionally convincing expression (e.g., realistic sleeping apostles, grief in Pietà) are judged positively; conveying believable human emotion via posture and face is a key criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of perspective / receding view
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'portrayed ... a most beautiful view receding in perspective, which was much extolled,' and made perspective a particular profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful use of linear perspective to create convincing spatial recession is a valued technical and aesthetic skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish and high finish (workmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work was 'brought to perfect completion with great loveliness and a high finish.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall finish — refinement of details, polish, and completeness — is an explicit criterion: a highly finished surface and careful completion mark excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour handling: freshness, vividness, and lighting ('lights')
rubrics_metrics.description: Pietro's works are praised for 'freshest colouring,' 'remained so fresh and vivid in colouring,' and an 'intelligent... understanding of colour, both in fresco and in oil... knowledge of the lights that are seen throughout his works.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour freshness, successful colour harmonies, and skilful handling of light and highlights (chiaroscuro/'lights') are central measures of quality in both fresco and oil media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper fresco technique (execute in buon fresco; avoid a secco retouch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works 'have remained beautiful... notwithstanding that it has been much exposed' because 'he did not retouch it on the dry, but used diligence in executing it well in fresco.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good fresco technique (painting on the wet plaster and avoiding extensive retouching when dry) is recommended to ensure durability and colour longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigment economy and handling (ultramarine technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Prior supplied ultramarine and watched it; Pietro demonstrated a technique of dipping the brush in a basin so that 'there remained more in the water than he had used on the picture,' later returning the pigment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical skill in using costly pigments (economy, correct mixing, and application technique) and reliable handling of pigments are practical criteria; anecdotes illustrate acceptable ways to use and account for expensive materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs fixed manner (variety of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pietro 'had reduced the theory of his art to a manner so fixed, that he made all his figures with the same expression,' which later drew censure when tastes changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a recognizable style can be positive, excessive repetitiveness (using the same figures/expressions repeatedly) is criticized; variety and responsiveness to new approaches are desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative detail and diligence in predella/small scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels and predella contained 'many scenes wrought very diligently with little figures' and small stories 'wrought with much diligence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful, detailed narrative work in predella panels and small-scale scenes demonstrates diligence and skill; judges note the quality of miniature episodes as indicative of overall craftsmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of thematic arrangement and meeting expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: An altar-piece arrangement offended critics: Pietro 'made the [Assumption] so commonplace, that the Deposition of Christ was placed in front' and when unveiled 'it received no little censure... particularly because Pietro had availed himself of those figures that he had been wont to use in other pictures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting subject placement, scale, and novelty to fit liturgical/patron expectations matters; deviation from expected thematic hierarchy or reuse of familiar figures can provoke criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with architectural setting and ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of churches include carved stone ornaments, lunettes, choirs, and panels by specific hands; paintings are discussed in relation to altars, choir positions, lunettes, and cloisters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment includes how well paintings and panels harmonize with architectural elements and liturgical furniture; successful integration with site (e.g., appropriate scale, subject for a lunette or altar) is a criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence across media (skill in both fresco and oil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pietro had an 'intelligent... understanding of colour, both in fresco and in oil,' and 'all experienced craftsmen are indebted to him' for knowledge of lights across media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versatility and mastery in multiple media (fresco and oil) is valued; technical knowledge that translates between media is a mark of a high-ranking craftsman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability and preservation of colour over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works 'have remained so fresh and vivid in colouring, painted as they are in fresco' and one oil panel 'has been preserved... as fresh as if it had only just been finished.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longevity of colour and resistance to environmental damage (exposure to rain, wind) are indicators of technical success; proper technique and suitable placement affect preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market success and patron recognition as indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Works were sold for large sums (a Sebastian sold to the King of France for four hundred gold ducats), and Pietro was summoned to Rome by the Pope; 'these works brought him a very great sum of money.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High payments, prestigious patrons, and wide geographic demand are treated as evidence of an artist's reputation and the perceived quality of his work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, influence, and creation of masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Pietro 'made many masters in his own manner,' and pupils like Raffaello surpassed him; his manner spread to France, Spain, Germany.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An artist's influence through pupils and the dissemination of his techniques/styles is a metric of importance and success; the ability to teach and spawn notable disciples counts as a form of achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism in anatomical depiction (bodily effects of time and suffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Pietà he 'made the Dead Christ all stiffened, as if He had been so long on the Cross that the length of time and the cold had reduced Him to this,' with supporting figures sorrowful and weeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Believable anatomical detail and rendering of physical effects (rigor mortis, weight, slack muscles) that enhance the emotional truth of the scene are praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallmarks and decorative signature motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists are noted for recurring motifs: Stefano's peacock is described as 'almost the hall-mark of pictures executed by him'; Bacchiaccha 'delighted in painting grotesques' and covered cabinets with animals and rare plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive decorative devices or recurring emblems (peacock, grotesques, particular ornamentation) function as signatures and can be considered positive markers of an identifiable workshop or master's hand.
